headline: Nvidia's slide and its first earnings report without Jensen Huang dominate a risk-off Tuesday, with chip export curbs, a cooling AI trade and a Deutsche Bank document leak adding to the pressure. Eli Lilly and J&J kept biotech dealmaking active, and the Anthropic IPO is expected this week.

paragraphs.text: Eli Lilly's buying spree continued. Endpoints and Fierce Biotech report a deal worth up to $5.9 billion with Cambridge, Massachusetts startup Stipple Bio to develop oncology drugs that target tumor cells more precisely. Lilly also agreed to pay $1.5 billion for Calytrix, which adds a myelofibrosis candidate. BioPharma Dive calls that the 15th acquisition this year, while Endpoints calls it the 14th, so the exact count is unclear. Either way the pace is well ahead of other big drugmakers, and Endpoints ties it to GLP-1 revenue.

paragraphs.text: Johnson & Johnson is buying eye-disease biotech Ollin Biosciences for $2.2 billion upfront, which Endpoints says could reach $3.3 billion with milestones. Fierce frames the Phase 3 bispecific as a challenge to Roche's Vabysmo, so the buyer takes on a crowded market. Smaller deals ran alongside. Biogen signed a pact worth up to $411 million with protein-degrader company TrimTech. Seawolf emerged with $100 million and an up-to-$1.2 billion Sanofi partnership. Novartis signed an antibody-drug conjugate deal worth over $2 billion, though only the headline is available. On the funding side, Flagship is putting £100 million into an AI-focused company-creation lab in London, and Sofinnova closed a €725 million crossover fund for later-stage biotechs. A Bristows note ties the M&A rebound to patent cliffs, and the day's deal flow fits that argument.

paragraphs.text: On the regulatory and clinical side, the FDA approved Roche's new breast cancer pill, which the company has said could become its top-selling product ever. AstraZeneca and Alexion won approval for Klygefa in generalized myasthenia gravis, entering a crowded market. Summit Therapeutics fell after the FDA rejected ivonescimab, refusing to look past its initial failure to extend survival in a form of lung cancer. CG Oncology's bladder cancer drug cut recurrence risk by 68% in Phase 3, well above expectations, and the stock rose. Helus Pharma's modified psilocybin hit its Phase 3 depression goals, though Endpoints says investors were slightly wary of the safety profile. Aclaris dropped its TSLP program after a Phase 2 eczema miss. Novo Nordisk rose premarket on weight-loss data and a European hemophilia approval, and its study in children as young as 6 worked for weight loss but raised questions about growth. The Alzheimer's news was weaker: a light-and-sound headset showed mixed results, and AriBio's repurposed erectile dysfunction drug gave tepid ones.

paragraphs.text: Policy news is mixed. NYT says hospitals are bracing for Medicaid work rules and deep funding cuts from Jan. 1, while Healthcare Dive reports CMS is letting states delay implementation through the end of June. The two reports sit uneasily together, so the real start date for individual states is worth checking. STAT says a new Trump rule aimed at fraud draws all its projected savings from Medicare Advantage, which matters for insurer exposure. John Powers III was made permanent head of NIAID. The FDA created a new regulatory category for the supplement NAC. Fierce reports the US has lost measles elimination status. CVS argues GLP-1s save employers money only at $350 a month or less, a clear signal to drugmakers on price. NYT also says US biotechs, wary of Chinese rivals, are sharing less about new ideas, a shift that could affect licensing dynamics.

paragraphs.text: Among providers, Allina Health and Sutter Health won Minnesota attorney general approval for a $26 billion combination creating a 39-hospital nonprofit system, targeting a Jan. 1 close. The Lown Institute found most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks exceeded their community spending in 2023, which could fuel scrutiny of such deals. At HLTH, CVS, Cigna and Abridge are working with OpenAI on agents that navigate record systems and payer portals. Google Cloud says healthcare is struggling to scale AI beyond pilots.

paragraphs.text: The AI trade is under strain heading into Nvidia's results. The Nasdaq 100 fell 2.7% on Monday, per the FT, and Bloomberg says Nvidia is down 35% from its October peak. Futures and European indexes were lower this morning. CNBC reports options are pricing a bigger-than-usual move, and analysts have cut price targets. This is Nvidia's first report since Jensen Huang resigned after an extramarital affair with an executive at a Singapore-based customer. The FT says the board is not considering bringing him back, while DealBook reports some in Silicon Valley want him reinstated and some in the Trump administration do not. The FT adds that Nvidia has set up a committee to oversee export-control compliance, and CNBC reports that scrutiny has reached Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his sons' firm's ties to the chipmaker.

paragraphs.text: Policy compounds the nerves. The NYT and others report the administration is closing a loophole in AI chip rules that would cut a data-center business serving Chinese firms, a move that has rattled Southeast Asia. The Commerce Department also says it is investigating Megaspeed over alleged chip smuggling, after criticism that it moved too slowly. The FT's editorial line is that controls need better enforcement, not a wider blockade. Sentiment is sour: the BofA survey shows the biggest cut in tech exposure since 2006, and 13F filings show some big funds were adding to Nvidia and megacap tech before the drawdown. Druckenmiller sold AMD and Sandisk while buying SpaceX and Palantir. The contrarian view is that the sell-off is justified but staying bearish may not be, since the FT points to a stronger case for hyperscalers. BTIG notes consumer staples rallied after the dot-com peak.

paragraphs.text: The Fed offers a balancing story. Chairman Kevin Warsh said the AI boom could support substantially higher US growth without stoking inflation, but also that it could disappoint, and he has set up a task force on labor-market effects. Gold held below $3,900 on bets the Fed raises rates next month, according to the Journal. Oil keeps falling on recovering Middle East exports and a forecast surplus, with US crude near $85. The US gasoline price hit an eight-month low, suggesting Iran-war inflation pressure is easing. Treasury and eurozone yields edged lower.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere, the UK jobless rate edged lower, and the FT says two-year gilt yields breached 5% on hawkish Bank of England messaging, which matches retail demand for long gilts yielding over 5%. German investor confidence rose to its highest since the Iran war began. Brussels raised eurozone growth forecasts on AI-driven exports, but halved France's. Germany nominated Markus Brunnermeier to the ECB board, clearing the way for Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos to head the bank. The New Zealand dollar hit a six-year low. China's October data missed on output, retail sales and investment. Canadian inflation held at 3.1%, and Governor Macklem will leave in June.

paragraphs.text: Private credit supplied most of the stress signals, though many items are thin. The Australian Financial Review says heightened redemptions have ASIC on high alert, and Trefis asks whether Golub Capital's $12.40 share price is private credit's first crack. Both are early signals, not conclusions. Meanwhile, Corebridge disclosed a 9.5% stake in a Carlyle tactical private credit fund and PGIM reported asset growth in its private credit fund. Money is still flowing in even as redemption questions build, so liquidity terms and marks need watching. Mike Milken's argument that private credit echoes the high-yield market's origins offers a bullish counterpoint.

paragraphs.text: Real estate lending is another weak spot. The Journal says big landlords such as Brookfield may be the readiest to cut losses on troubled apartment properties, leaving lenders burned. Its newsletter flags souring apartment deals. Delaware Life Insurance, linked to Dodgers owner Mark Walter, cut affiliated holdings to 35% of assets but missed its target. On the consumer side, the Journal says households are using home equity lines to pay down credit cards and buy cars, to avoid giving up low-rate first mortgages.

paragraphs.text: The FT reports banks are trying to offload debt tied to data centers and chips as public opposition threatens some mega projects. This matters as AI equity sentiment sours, because lender appetite for the build-out is a real constraint. In structured credit, a Jay-Z-backed music rights firm raised nearly $700 million backed by a securitization of royalties, which shows investors still want steady yield outside traditional markets. Monroe Capital backed OceanSound Partners' investment in IMSAR, a small sponsor-finance example. A startup called Forward raised $1.5 million to route private credit deals to suitable funds.

paragraphs.text: The Anthropic IPO is the main event, expected this week. New Street Research initiated at buy with a $105 price target, and CNBC says derivatives show bullish signs in a proxy trade. NeoTeo reports orders at six times the shares on offer. That is a single secondary source, so treat it cautiously. Danish pension fund PKA is set for a gain of about a billion kroner, per AMWatch. Bloomberg says Anthropic's compute dilemma is its biggest IPO risk. The timing is awkward, with the AI trade under pressure and Nvidia reporting, so pricing and day-one trading will test appetite for the theme. Core Specialty's IPO is also in the news, with the company saying it aims to raise its profile and improve future access to equity markets, though the details are thin.

paragraphs.text: Deutsche Bank is the day's main banking story. The FT, working from 15 million leaked documents, says the bank processed $582 million of suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein and that the figure is far larger than previously known. The Journal reports allegations that the bank courted Russian oligarchs before the Ukraine invasion. The FT also describes problems under CEO Christian Sewing, including a 2017 data breach that leaked Trump's tax statements. MarketWatch says as much as €3.8 billion of market value was wiped out. Whether the shares recover depends on regulatory and legal follow-up, which the list does not yet cover.

Iceye launched a €2 billion bid for Italian rocket maker Avio to build an integrated European space and defense group. Princes agreed an €80 million purchase of four French food brands from Mondelez. Rothschild & Co is anchoring its growth plan in Italy, aiming past €200 billion in wealth and asset management assets by 2030.
